title: Ezekiel 12:17–28
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to eat and drink with trembling as a sign of the fear that will grip Jerusalem and the land because of its violence. The LORD then answers two sayings about delay. The first, “The days are prolonged, and every vision fails,” treats prophecy as unreliable; the LORD replaces it with “The days are at hand, and the fulfillment of every vision.” The second grants the prophecy but says it concerns times far off; the LORD answers that none of his words will be deferred any longer. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the certainty of God’s word and the danger of mistaking his patience for delay.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel again. A second sign-act follows.

Arminian readers see God continuing to warn through vivid actions, giving the people more than one opportunity to grasp what is coming.
verses.reformedNotes:
This short sign-act shifts from the king’s flight to the people’s daily life.

Reformed readers see God patiently repeating his message. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the persistence of God’s warnings to a people slow to believe them.

verses.text: “Son of man, eat your bread with quaking, and drink your water with trembling and with fearfulness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to eat his bread with quaking and drink his water with trembling. Fear becomes the sign.

Arminian readers see the prophet embodying the anxiety that will grip the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sign-act may involve a visible trembling as he eats, though the text does not describe the performance in detail.

Reformed readers see the prophet bearing the message in his body. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the coming distress and keep the description hedged.

verses.text: Tell the people of the land, ‘The Lord GOD says concerning the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the land of Israel: “They will eat their bread with fearfulness and drink their water in dismay, that her land may be desolate, and all that is therein, because of the violence of all those who dwell therein.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is to tell the people that Jerusalem’s inhabitants will eat with fearfulness and drink in dismay, because of the violence of those who live there. The cause is violence.

Arminian readers see consequences tied to injustice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse links the land’s desolation to the violence within it.

Reformed readers see God’s justice responding to violence. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the moral roots of the coming disaster.

verses.text: The cities that are inhabited will be laid waste, and the land will be a desolation. Then you will know that I am the LORD.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Inhabited cities will be laid waste and the land desolate, and then they will know that the LORD is God. Judgment reveals God.

Arminian readers see the consequences of persistent violence and rebellion against God’s warnings.
verses.reformedNotes:
The refrain again ties judgment to the knowledge of God.

Reformed readers see God vindicating his name through judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of judgment and its purpose of revealing the LORD to his people.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel once more. A new saying is addressed.

Arminian readers see God confronting the people’s thinking directly, not only their actions, so that their excuses are answered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Two related sayings follow in 12:21–25 and 12:26–28, both about delay.

Reformed readers see God answering human doubt with his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s concern to correct false ideas that keep people from responding to his warnings.

verses.text: “Son of man, what is this proverb that you have in the land of Israel, saying, ‘The days are prolonged, and every vision fails’?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks about the proverb in Israel: “The days are prolonged, and every vision fails.” Skepticism has become a saying.

Arminian readers see delay used as an excuse not to respond.
verses.reformedNotes:
The proverb treats past prophetic warnings as unfulfilled and therefore unreliable.

Reformed readers see unbelief mocking God’s patience. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of mistaking God’s patience for absence or weakness.

verses.text: Tell them therefore, ‘The Lord GOD says: “I will make this proverb to cease, and they will no more use it as a proverb in Israel;” ’ but tell them, ‘ “The days are at hand, and the fulfillment of every vision.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD will end the proverb and replace it with another: “The days are at hand, and the fulfillment of every vision.” The saying is reversed.

Arminian readers see a final warning against complacency.
verses.reformedNotes:
The replacement saying answers the old proverb phrase by phrase.

Reformed readers see God’s word overturning human sayings. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the certainty of God’s word, whose fulfillment may be delayed but will not fail.

verses.text: For there will be no more any false vision nor flattering divination within the house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
There will be no more false vision or flattering divination in Israel. False voices will be silenced.

Arminian readers see the removal of voices that encouraged complacency and kept the people from taking God’s warnings seriously.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse anticipates chapter 13’s condemnation of false prophets.

Reformed readers see God purifying prophecy. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the harm done by flattering messages that tell people what they want to hear, and God’s intention to end them.

verses.text: For I am the LORD. I will speak, and the word that I speak will be performed. It will be no more deferred; for in your days, rebellious house, I will speak the word and will perform it,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says the word he speaks will be performed and no longer deferred; in their days he will speak and perform it. The delay ends.

Arminian readers see the window for response narrowing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse stresses that God’s word is not empty speech.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign faithfulness to his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reliability of what God says, which will be fulfilled in the hearers’ own lifetime.

verses.text: Again the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel again. A second saying about delay is addressed.

Arminian readers see God answering another form of evasion, one that accepts the prophecy but places it far in the future.
verses.reformedNotes:
This saying differs from the first: it does not deny the visions but pushes them into the distant future.

Reformed readers see God addressing every form of resistance to his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “Son of man, behold, they of the house of Israel say, ‘The vision that he sees is for many days to come, and he prophesies of times that are far off.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The house of Israel says, “The vision that he sees is for many days to come, and he prophesies of times that are far off.” The prophecy is postponed in their minds.

Arminian readers see a subtle evasion of personal responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
This view grants the prophet’s message but denies its urgency.

Reformed readers see the heart avoiding God’s claim. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of treating God’s warnings as distant.

verses.text: “Therefore tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “None of my words will be deferred any more, but the word which I speak will be performed,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says none of his words will be deferred any longer; the word he speaks will be performed. The answer is final.

Arminian readers see an urgent call to respond now.
verses.reformedNotes:
The closing verse repeats the point of verse 25, answering both sayings about delay with the same assurance.

Reformed readers see God’s word sure to be fulfilled. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the urgency and reliability of God’s word.
